lessons.title: When to Irrigate: Critical Growth Stages
lessons.body: Wheat and barley need water most at three stages: tillering (3-4 weeks after planting), stem elongation to booting (6-8 weeks), and grain filling (10-12 weeks). In dry African conditions, missing water at these stages can cut your yield by half. For example, in Ethiopia's Arsi region, wheat needs about 450-650 mm of water per season. If rainfall is less than 20 mm per week, you must irrigate. Check your soil: if you can't squeeze a ball of soil into a ribbon, it's too dry. At tillering, irrigate when the top 15 cm of soil is dry. At booting, the crop uses 5-7 mm of water per day. At grain filling, don't let the soil dry out completelyâwater stress now shrinks the grains. In sandy soils, irrigate every 5-7 days; in clay soils, every 10-14 days. A simple way: dig a hole 15 cm deep. If the soil at the bottom is dry, irrigate. Avoid irrigating at middayâearly morning or evening reduces evaporation. Also, avoid overwatering: waterlogged soil at tillering can cause yellowing. For barley, critical stages are similar but it tolerates drought a bit better. In Kenya's Narok County, farmers use the 'look and feel' method: if the leaves roll and the soil is dusty, irrigate immediately. Remember, one deep watering is better than several light sprinkles. Deep watering encourages roots to grow down. If you have a moisture meter (cost about $20), keep soil moisture above 50% at critical stages. Without a meter, use a stick: push a wooden stick into the soil. If it comes out dry, irrigate. Always record rainfall and irrigation dates in a notebook to learn your farm's pattern.

lessons.title: Bucket, Drip, and Sprinkler Systems for Small Farms
lessons.body: For a small farm of 0.5 to 2 hectares, you don't need expensive machinery. Start with a bucket system: 20-litre buckets with small holes in the bottom. Place one bucket next to each plant or along a row. Fill it once a day. This works for vegetables but for wheat and barley, it's too slow. Better: drip irrigation. A simple drip kit for 500 plants costs about $50. You need a 200-litre drum raised 1 meter high, a filter (old cloth works), and 16 mm drip tape. Lay the tape along rows, with emitters every 30 cm. This saves 60% water compared to flooding. In Zimbabwe, farmers use 'bucket drip' kits: a bucket with a micro-tube to each plant. For 1 hectare of wheat, you need about 10,000 meters of drip tape, costing $300-$500. That's too much for many. So consider sprinklers. A small sprinkler (impact type) covers a 12-meter circle. You need a pump (petrol or solar) and pipes. A 1-inch pump costs $150. You can move it every 30 minutes. For barley, sprinklers work well. But sprinklers lose water to wind and evaporationâirrigate early morning. A cheaper option: use a watering can (10 litres) to water the base of plants. One person can water 0.1 hectare in 2 hours. For 1 hectare, you need 100 hoursânot practical. So combine methods: use drip for seed production and sprinklers for grain. In northern Nigeria, farmers use 'shaduf' (a lever with a bucket) to lift water from shallow wells. That's free but labor-intensive. Always check your water source: a well or borehole must yield at least 1 litre per second to irrigate 1 hectare. Test by filling a 20-litre bucket and timing it. If it takes more than 20 seconds, your yield is too low for sprinklers. Drip is more forgiving. Start small: 0.1 hectare with drip, then expand.

lessons.title: Harvesting Rainwater with Ponds and Tanks
lessons.body: In many parts of Africa, rain comes in short, heavy storms. You can capture that water for dry spells. A farm pond (also called a water pan) is a shallow hole lined with clay or plastic. Dig it at the lowest point of your field, 2-3 meters deep, with sides sloping at 45 degrees. A pond 10m x 10m x 2m holds 200,000 litresâenough to irrigate 0.2 hectares of wheat for 10 days. Line the bottom with a 1mm plastic sheet (cost about $100 for 100 square meters) to stop seepage. Cover it with a thin layer of soil to protect from sunlight. For smaller needs, use tanks. A 5,000-litre plastic tank costs $300. Place it under a roof gutter. A 10m x 10m iron sheet roof catches 1,000 litres from 10 mm of rain. So a 20 mm storm gives 2,000 litres. In Kenya's semi-arid areas, farmers use 'rock catchments': natural rock surfaces that channel water into tanks. You can also dig a 'half-moon' micro-catchment: a semicircular bund 2 meters wide, with the open side facing uphill. This catches runoff for a single tree or a small plot. For wheat, you need about 500 litres per square meter over the season. So a 10m x 10m plot needs 50,000 litres. A pond of 100,000 litres can support two such plots. Always keep ponds fenced to stop animals. Add a silt trap: a small pit before the pond where soil settles. Clean the pond yearly. In Ethiopia, the 'trench' system: dig trenches 50 cm deep and 30 cm wide along contours, spaced 5 meters apart. They catch rain and let it soak in. This is cheaper than a pond. For tanks, use first-flush diverter: a small pipe that throws away the first 10 minutes of rain, which carries dirt. Then water enters the tank. Use a mesh screen to keep out leaves. Store water in dark tanks to reduce algae. Test water for salt before using on wheatâbarley tolerates salt better.

lessons.title: Drainage Channels to Prevent Waterlogging
lessons.body: Wheat and barley hate wet feet. If water stands in your field for more than 2 days, roots rot and yield drops. In high-rainfall areas like the highlands of Kenya or Ethiopia, you must drain excess water. The simplest method: open ditches. Dig channels 30 cm deep and 30 cm wide, running downhill. Space them every 10-15 meters. In flat fields, make them every 5 meters. The water flows to a lower area or a pond. For a 1-hectare field, you need about 200 meters of ditch. Dig them before the rains start. Use a hoe and shovelâtwo people can dig 50 meters in a day. Line the ditch with grass or stones to stop erosion. In clay soils, water moves slowly, so make ditches deeper (50 cm) and closer (every 8 meters). In sandy soils, ditches can be wider apart. Another method: raised beds. Make beds 1 meter wide and 20 cm high, with furrows between. This is common for barley in the Ethiopian highlands. The furrows carry water away. For wheat, you can also use 'broad beds and furrows': beds 2 meters wide, furrows 30 cm deep. This works well with a tractor or oxen. If you have a slope, use 'graded ditches': they run across the slope at a slight angle (0.5%) so water flows slowly without eroding. Check ditches after every storm. Remove silt and blockages. In Nigeria's derived savannah, farmers use 'bed and furrow' to grow wheat in the dry season with irrigation, and the furrows also drain excess rain. A cheap test for waterlogging: dig a hole 30 cm deep, fill with water, and see how long it takes to drain. If more than 24 hours, you need drainage. Also, look for yellowing leaves and stunted growth after rain. For small plots, just make a shallow trench around the plot. Remember, drainage water can be stored in a pond for later use. Never let drainage water run off your farmâcatch it. In South Africa, farmers use 'stormwater drains' with grassed waterways. Keep ditches clear of crops. Plant grass on the edges to hold soil.

lessons.title: Mulching to Conserve Soil Moisture
lessons.body: Mulch is any material you spread on the soil surface to stop water from evaporating. In dry African conditions, mulching can reduce water loss by 50-70%. For wheat and barley, apply mulch after planting but before the crop covers the ground. Use crop residues: maize stalks, straw, or grass. Spread a layer 5-10 cm thick. One hectare needs about 5-10 tonnes of dry mulch. That's a lot, but you can start with 2 tonnes on the most exposed areas. In Kenya's Laikipia County, farmers use 'straw mulch' from previous barley crops. After harvest, keep the straw and spread it back. This also adds organic matter. For small plots, use leaves, banana leaves, or even stones. A stone mulch (rocks 5-10 cm) works well in dry areasâit cools the soil and reduces evaporation. In the Sahel, farmers use 'zai' pits: dig holes 20 cm deep, fill with manure, and cover with mulch. This concentrates water and nutrients. For wheat, mulch between rows. Be careful: thick mulch can hide pests like termites. In Ethiopia, farmers use 'trash lines': lines of crop residue along contours. These slow runoff and let water soak in. Mulch also stops weeds, but some weeds grow through. Hand-weed before mulching. If you have livestock, don't use all residues for mulchâfeed some to animals. A compromise: mulch half the field. In sandy soils, mulch is critical because water drains fast. In clay soils, mulch prevents crusting. You can also use plastic mulch: black plastic sheeting (30 microns thick) laid on beds. It costs about $200 per hectare but lasts 2-3 seasons. It warms soil and stops evaporation. For barley in cool highlands, plastic mulch can boost yields. But plastic is not biodegradableâremove and reuse. A cheaper option: living mulch, like clover, but it competes for water. So stick to dead mulch. Apply mulch after rain when soil is moist. If you mulch dry soil, it stays dry. Test: dig under mulch after 3 daysâsoil should be damp. Without mulch, it will be dry. Mulching also reduces soil temperature by 5-10Â°C, which helps roots. In Zimbabwe, farmers use 'muchero' (leaf litter) from mopane trees. Collect it in the dry season. One wheelbarrow covers 10 square meters. For 0.1 hectare, you need 100 wheelbarrowsâtoo much. So focus on seedbeds or high-value areas. Combine mulch with drip irrigation for best results.

lessons.title: Scheduling Irrigation Without Expensive Tools
lessons.body: You don't need a $500 soil moisture meter. Use these free or cheap methods. First, the 'feel method': take a handful of soil from 15 cm deep. Squeeze it. If it forms a ball that holds together but doesn't leave your hand wet, it's moist enough. If it crumbles, irrigate. If it drips water, it's too wet. Practice this daily. Second, the 'stick method': push a smooth wooden stick (like a broom handle) into the soil. If it goes in easily, soil is moist. If it's hard to push, irrigate. Third, the 'evaporation pan': a simple pan (like a frying pan) painted black, filled with water, placed in the field. Measure how much water evaporates in 24 hours. If it's more than 5 mm, irrigate. You can make a cheap pan from a tin can. Fourth, 'crop signs': wheat leaves roll inward at midday when thirsty. Barley turns a dull green. If you see these, irrigate within 24 hours. Fifth, 'rainfall records': keep a rain gauge (a simple plastic tube with markings, cost $5). Write down daily rainfall. If you get less than 20 mm in a week, irrigate. For scheduling, use the 'checkbook' method: your soil holds about 100 mm of water per meter depth. Wheat uses 5 mm per day. So after 10 days without rain, you need 50 mm of irrigation. A simple rule: irrigate every 7-10 days in sandy soil, every 10-14 days in clay. For drip, run the system for 1-2 hours every 2 days. For sprinklers, apply 20 mm per irrigation. To know when to stop, dig a hole after irrigation: water should reach 30 cm deep. If not, irrigate longer. In Ethiopia, farmers use 'tensiometers' made from a bottle and a tubeâbut that's advanced. Stick to the feel method. Also, group your fields: irrigate the thirstiest first. Keep a notebook: date, rainfall, irrigation amount, crop stage. After one season, you'll know your farm's pattern. In Kenya's Narok, farmers use the 'moon' method: irrigate at full moon? No, that's myth. Use science. Finally, check the forecast: if rain is predicted in 2 days, wait. But don't wait too longâwheat at booting can't wait. A simple test: if you can't push a stick 10 cm into the soil, irrigate now.

quiz.q: At which growth stage does wheat need water most?
quiz.explanation: Tillering is one of the critical stages where water stress can severely reduce yield.

quiz.q: How deep should you check soil moisture for wheat irrigation?
quiz.explanation: The top 15 cm is where most roots are active and indicates when to irrigate.

quiz.q: What is a simple sign that wheat needs irrigation?
quiz.explanation: Leaf rolling is a clear sign of water stress in wheat and barley.

quiz.q: How often should you irrigate sandy soil in dry conditions?
quiz.explanation: Sandy soils drain quickly, so they need more frequent irrigation.

quiz.q: Which irrigation method saves the most water?
quiz.explanation: Drip irrigation delivers water directly to roots, reducing evaporation and runoff.

quiz.q: What is the approximate cost of a simple drip kit for 500 plants?
quiz.explanation: A basic drip kit for 500 plants costs around $50, making it affordable for small farms.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid irrigating at midday?
quiz.explanation: Midday heat causes high evaporation, wasting water.

quiz.q: What is a 'shaduf'?
options: B) A lever with a bucket
quiz.explanation: A shaduf is a traditional manual water-lifting device used in Africa.

quiz.q: How much water does a 10m x 10m x 2m pond hold?
quiz.explanation: Volume = 10 x 10 x 2 = 200 cubic meters = 200,000 litres.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a silt trap before a pond?
quiz.explanation: A silt trap lets soil settle before water enters the pond, keeping it clean.

quiz.q: How much water can a 10m x 10m roof catch from 10 mm of rain?
quiz.explanation: 10m x 10m = 100 mÂ²; 10 mm = 0.01 m; volume = 1 mÂ³ = 1,000 litres.

quiz.q: Which crop tolerates salt better?
quiz.explanation: Barley is more salt-tolerant than wheat, making it suitable for saline water.

quiz.q: What is a half-moon micro-catchment?
quiz.explanation: A half-moon is a semicircular earth bund that catches runoff for a small area.

quiz.q: How deep should drainage ditches be in clay soil?
quiz.explanation: Clay soils drain slowly, so deeper ditches (50 cm) are needed.

quiz.q: What is a sign of waterlogging in wheat?
quiz.explanation: Yellowing leaves and stunted growth indicate waterlogged roots.

quiz.q: How can you test if soil is waterlogged?
options: A) Dig a hole and fill with water
quiz.explanation: If water in a 30 cm hole takes more than 24 hours to drain, drainage is poor.

quiz.q: What is a 'broad bed and furrow' system?
quiz.explanation: Broad beds and furrows help drain excess water and are common in Ethiopian highlands.

quiz.q: Why should drainage water be stored?
quiz.explanation: Drainage water can be captured in ponds and used during dry spells.

quiz.q: What is the recommended mulch thickness for moisture conservation?
quiz.explanation: A 5-10 cm layer of mulch effectively reduces evaporation without smothering crops.

quiz.q: Which material is a good mulch in dry areas?
quiz.explanation: Stones act as mulch, cooling soil and reducing evaporation in dry regions.

quiz.q: What is a 'zai' pit?
options: A) A planting hole with manure and mulch
quiz.explanation: Zai pits concentrate water and nutrients for crops in the Sahel.

quiz.q: Why should you apply mulch after rain?
quiz.explanation: Mulching after rain traps existing moisture in the soil.

quiz.q: What is a cheap tool to measure rainfall?
quiz.explanation: A simple rain gauge costs about $5 and helps track rainfall for irrigation scheduling.

quiz.q: What does the 'feel method' test?
quiz.explanation: Squeezing soil in your hand indicates moisture level.

quiz.q: How much water does wheat use per day during booting?
quiz.explanation: Wheat uses about 5-7 mm of water per day at booting stage.

quiz.q: What is the 'checkbook' method for irrigation scheduling?
options: A) Using a notebook to track water balance
quiz.explanation: The checkbook method tracks rainfall and water use to decide when to irrigate.

quiz.q: How deep should irrigation water reach for wheat?
quiz.explanation: Water should penetrate at least 30 cm to reach the root zone.

quiz.q: Which is a sign that you should NOT irrigate?
options: C) Rain is forecast in 2 days
quiz.explanation: If rain is expected soon, you can save water and wait.

quiz.q: What is a simple stick test for soil moisture?
options: A) Push a stick into soil
quiz.explanation: If a wooden stick pushes easily into soil, moisture is adequate.

quiz.q: Why is mulching important in sandy soils?
quiz.explanation: Mulch reduces evaporation and helps sandy soil retain moisture longer.
